title: Tired of Waiting for a Green Card, Indian H-1B Workers Are Hedging With the UK
excerpt: With the EB-2 India green card backlog stretching to 14 years and H-1B uncertainty mounting, a growing number of Indian tech professionals are pursuing UK Global Talent Visas as a parallel immigration strategy.
body:
• The April 2026 US Visa Bulletin set the EB-2 India priority date at July 2014, meaning a 14-year wait for a green card, while the UK Global Talent Visa offers settlement in as little as three years.
  • London-based immigration firms report rising inquiries from Indian H-1B holders in San Francisco and Seattle exploring the UK route as a backup plan.
  • Unlike the H-1B, the UK Global Talent Visa requires no employer sponsorship, has no annual cap, and allows holders to change jobs, freelance, or start businesses freely.
  • Indian professionals are treating immigration as a "risk-management exercise," maintaining US plans while building UK options alongside them.

The Arithmetic of Leaving

Yash Dubal, CEO of London-based A Y & J Solicitors, frames the decision in the bluntest terms he can: "The April 2026 Visa Bulletin set the EB-2 India date at July 2014, which means a fourteen-year wait for a green card. The UK Global Talent Visa gets you to settlement in three. It is not a more emotional decision than that. It is arithmetic."

Dubal told The American Bazaar that the shift is being driven largely by highly skilled Indian professionals who have spent years waiting for permanent residency in the United States. Most of his firm's US inquiries come from Indian engineers and researchers, often in their thirties, on H-1B visas. Their spouses hold H-4 visas, their children are US-born, and they have been waiting on green cards for years.

The trend accelerated after the Trump administration announced a $100,000 H-1B visa fee in September 2025 — a move that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley. Although an appeals court in Boston blocked the fee's collection in late July 2026, the political volatility has not subsided.

"Indian professionals are no longer treating uncertainty in the US as a temporary problem to wait out. They are treating it as a feature of the system and acting accordingly."

— Yash Dubal, CEO, A Y & J Solicitors

Why the UK Global Talent Visa

Introduced in 2020 as part of Britain's post-Brexit immigration system, the Global Talent Visa has gained traction for its structural advantages over the H-1B pathway. The visa is tied to the individual rather than an employer. Holders can work for any company, change jobs without reapplying, freelance, consult, or start a business. There is no minimum salary requirement, no job offer requirement, and no employer sponsorship needed.

For Indian professionals, the most compelling feature is the timeline. Applicants endorsed as "exceptional talent" can apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain — the UK equivalent of a green card — after just three years. Those endorsed for "exceptional promise" qualify in five years. British citizenship becomes available one year after that.

Immigration experts note the UK's costs are a fraction of the US system. Chetal Patel, head of immigration at London law firm Bates Wells, told Personnel Today that UK sponsors pay an Immigration Skills Charge ranging from £364 to £1,000 per year — compared to the now-blocked $100,000 H-1B fee in the United States.

Not Abandoning America — Building a Hedge

Immigration lawyers stress that most Indian professionals pursuing UK visas are not giving up on the US. They are running parallel strategies.

"Indian H-1B holders are not abandoning the US plan," Dubal said. "They are putting a UK plan alongside it, as a hedge. The choice between three years to UK settlement and another decade of uncertainty in the US becomes harder to defer once it is sitting on the page."

The pattern is familiar to corporate employers as well. Market analysis suggests that some US companies with UK offices are proactively relocating talent to London to avoid H-1B lottery failures. The UK tech ecosystem is, as a result, capturing senior talent that would otherwise remain in Silicon Valley.

"The lifeblood of talent flowing into US industries is being diverted, and countries like the UK are poised to pick up the pieces."

— Chetal Patel, Bates Wells

The Qualification Question

The Global Talent Visa is not a blanket alternative. Applicants must first obtain an endorsement from an approved UK body — for tech professionals, this is typically Tech Nation — before submitting their visa application. The endorsement process evaluates whether the applicant is a recognized leader or shows exceptional promise in their field.

But Dubal believes many Indian professionals underestimate how close they already are to qualifying. "Indian engineers applying to us are often closer to qualifying than they assume," he said. The typical profile — a senior engineer with publications, patents, or significant industry contributions — often aligns well with the endorsement criteria.

A Broader Shift

The US-to-UK pipeline is part of a larger realignment in global talent flows. Canada's Express Entry system and Australia's General Skilled Migration program remain popular alternatives for Indian professionals. But the UK's English-language environment, established Indian diaspora, and proximity to European markets give it distinct appeal for tech workers weighing their options.

For the estimated 300,000 Indians currently on H-1B visas in the United States, the calculation Dubal describes is increasingly hard to ignore. The question is no longer whether to plan for life beyond the green card backlog, but where.
